newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU ministers agree road traffic pollution deal.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers agree road traffic pollution deal.

text.p: European Union environment ministers boosted chances of an earlier-than-planned cut in traffic fumes on Friday when they tightened parts of a draft package of engine emission and fuel quality standards for cars.
"It's a real step forward and I am very proud of the fact that agreement was reached on this," Dutch Environment Minister Margreeth de Boer told a news conference early on Friday.
De Boer, whose country holds the EU presidency, chaired the talks to a unanimous deal.
"It means that we will get to our air quality objectives quicker," one European Commission official said of the result.

Planned measures from the so-called Auto/Oil proposals will cost industry five billion European currency units per year ($5.7 billion) from 2000 and six billion ecus per year for the five years from 2006, a Dutch official said.

Friday's changes, if made law, would add maybe 500 million ecus per year to projected costs for improved fuel norms and between 30 and 50 ecus to the cost of new vehicles from 2002 for the introduction of a planned cold-start test of car emissions.

On the table before ministers were two Commission proposals drawn up after years of research work with the European oil and car industries and launched last year amid widespread criticism of the standards set and methods used.
De Boer said the ministers from newly elected governments in Britain and France helped swing the meeting behind tougher cuts.

Ministers cut from 200 parts per million to 150 parts per million (ppm) proposed mandatory limits on the sulphur to be allowed in petrol from the year 2000, a move which will curb the damaging effects of sulphur dioxide on catalytic converters fitted to car exhausts.

But they included an opt-out, which Greece and Portugal said they would definitely take up, allowing countries to stay the application of new standards for up to three years in the case of "severe socio-economic problems".
Ministers also halved allowed benzene levels in petrol to one percent from the year 2000, meaning reduced airborne pollution by the cancer-causing chemical.

Friday's deal, which must win the approval of the European Parliament before adoption, also cut proposed 2000 limits for aromatics and set 2005 as the cut-off date for derogations to a year-2000 ban on leaded petrol.
It also set indicative fuel norms for 2005, including 50 ppm for sulphur in petrol and a "gradual phase-in and distribution" of 50 ppm diesel from the same date.
On engine emission norms, ministers retained proposed limit values for 2000 and 2005 while pushing a planned Commission progress review back six months to mid-1999.

Member states wishing to encourage early sales of new engine technologies may offer tax incentives from the vehicle proposals' final adoption, linked first to the 2000 targets until they come into force and then to the 2005 ones.
Ministers also reached a deal on rules intended to limit polluting emissions of volatile organic chemicals from industrial processes such as pharmaceutical manufacturing and car-body paint spraying.
